result.summary: Suppliants gather before the palace at Thebes, begging King Oedipus to end a plague. Oedipus says he has sent Creon to Delphi, and Creon returns with Apollo's answer: the murderers of the old king Laius must be found. Oedipus vows to track them down.

scenes.title: The Priest's Plea
scenes.summary: Oedipus finds suppliants at his door. The Priest describes the plague and asks him to save Thebes again. Oedipus says he has already sent Creon to Delphi.
scenes.stakes: Thebes is dying of plague, and Oedipus's standing as saviour of the city is at risk.

place.name: Before the Palace of Oedipus at Thebes

scenes.title: Creon Brings Apollo's Answer
scenes.summary: Creon arrives and reports that Apollo demands the killers of Laius be driven out or punished. Oedipus questions him about Laius's death and vows to find the culprits.
scenes.stakes: Until Laius's killers are found the plague continues, and Oedipus fears the killer may also strike at him.

alias_notes.explanation: Phoebus and Loxias are epithets of Apollo, god of the Delphic oracle.
Loxias is a title of Apollo as speaker of oracles.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable statement that a city is nothing without its people.

analysis.text: The opening shows Oedipus as a confident, caring ruler, setting up the irony that the killer he hunts is himself.
Plague as divine pollution reflects Greek belief that unpunished bloodshed defiled a whole community, and oracles like Delphi guided public decisions.

legacy.text: Sophocles' play inspired Freud's term Oedipus complex and has been a model for dramatic irony.

fun_facts.text: This is a verse translation by Gilbert Murray, using rhymed couplets rather than Sophocles' Greek metre.

language_notes.text: "Fruit of Cadmus' ancient tree" means descendants of Cadmus, Thebes' legendary founder; "wherefore" means why, and "ye" is the plural "you."
"The Slayer" is the plague-god or death itself; the prayers and shrieks are meant to frighten it away. "Withal" means besides.
Athena's two temples and the ash at the shore of Ismenus refer to Theban holy places, where the fire-altars gave omens by their ashes.
The "trough" is the hollow between waves; the ship cannot lift its prow above them.
"Hell's house" is the underworld, the house of Hades, which grows rich with the dead the plague sends.
The Sphinx's song was her riddle; Thebes paid a tribute of lives to her until Oedipus solved it.
"Eke" means also. The Priest suggests Oedipus may have heard divine voices or a man's advice, since the experienced find counsel in every event.
The "bird of old" is the good omen, as birds were read for signs, that brought Oedipus' earlier success.
Apollo's House in Delphi is the god's oracle, where questions about the gods' will were answered by the priestess.
"At point of time" means "at the right moment"; the Priest says Oedipus speaks just as Creon appears.
"His seemings" means his outward appearance; Oedipus prays that the god's guidance will make Creon's news as happy as he looks.
A wreath of fruited laurel, sacred to Apollo, signals good news from the god's oracle.
"Clear-voiced" means a person with a carrying voice; Oedipus says Creon is near enough to hear a shout.
"Annoy" here means harm or trouble, much stronger than the modern sense.
Phoebus is a title of Apollo, meaning "bright"; Loxias, used later, is another title linked to his oracles.
"Unclean thing" means a pollution: the guilt of unavenged murder was thought to infect the land.
"Pilot us" means steer the city as a ship's captain would; Oedipus came to rule Thebes after Laius.
"Withal" means "with it all" or "besides"; "blurred trail" and "ancient stain" refer to the old, faded guilt of the murder.
"Amain" means with full force or vigor; the sense is that diligent seekers find what they hunt, while neglected matters slip away.
"Dark-songed" refers to the Sphinx's riddling, ominous song; she plagued Thebes before Oedipus solved her riddle.
Phoebus is Apollo, whose oracle at Delphi gave the answer Creon has brought.
"Succour" means to help or relieve someone in distress.
Suppliant boughs were olive or laurel branches, wreathed in wool, laid on altars by those begging the gods for help.

context_notes.text: Suppliants carried olive branches wrapped in wool to show they were begging for help, and they sat at altars for protection.
Oedipus became king by defeating the Sphinx, which had terrorised Thebes; he was then a stranger to the city.
Creon is the brother of Jocasta, Oedipus' wife and queen of Thebes.
Creon is Jocasta's brother and thus Oedipus's brother-in-law; his father was Menoikeus.
Laius, former king of Thebes, was killed on a journey. His murderers were never found.
Delphi was Apollo's famous oracle site, where people sought divine guidance. Laius was travelling there when he was killed.
One attendant survived the attack and later fled; he becomes an important witness in the play.
The Sphinx was a monster that terrorized Thebes with a riddle and killed those who failed to answer, distracting the city from Laius's murder.

literary_notes.text: The city is a storm-battered ship sinking in waves of death, an image of a state in crisis.
The plague becomes a burning, loathly god that lights upon the land and sweeps it.
Praising Oedipus as a stranger who knew nothing yet saved them foreshadows the truth about his origins.
Walls, towers and ships are set against men, stressing that a city is its people.
Oedipus presents himself as a king who suffers more than any subject, showing his sympathy and pride.
Oedipus vows to follow any task the god gives, not knowing it will bring his own ruin.
Oedipus says he is neither hot nor cold, meaning Creon's vague, hopeful words leave him unmoved and impatient for plain facts.
Oedipus shows himself a ruler who cares more for his people's suffering than for his own safety.
Oedipus says he never saw Laius's face, unaware that he met and killed Laius; the audience may sense the coming horror.
Oedipus reasons that only an inside plot could explain such bold robbers, unknowingly pointing toward the truth about himself.
Oedipus fears the killer may attack him too, unaware he is himself the killer and that his care for Laius is literally for his own kin.
Oedipus's choice between greatness crowned or cast down anticipates his eventual fall.
